The Rhône River. A major western European river flowing five hundred and five miles from the Swiss Alps through Lake Geneva and eastern France into the Mediterranean Sea. It is the fastest and most powerful river in France, draining the Alps and creating the fertile Rhône delta.

The Rhône originates in the Swiss Alps and flows northwest through Lake Geneva, also known as Lac Léman, the largest freshwater lake in western Europe. It exits Lake Geneva at Geneva and flows south through the Rhône valley, accelerating as it descends. Its current is notably fast and dangerous. The Rhône delta in southern France, known as the Camargue, is a vast wetland and salt-marsh region known for wild horses, flamingos, and unique ecosystems found nowhere else in Europe. The river empties into the Mediterranean near Marseille. In Roman times, it was a crucial transport artery for north-south Mediterranean trade, connecting northern Europe to Rome and the wider Mediterranean world.

The Rhône has historically been difficult to navigate due to its rapids and strong current. Medieval and Renaissance river management attempted to build locks and channels to improve navigation. The Rhône valley is a major wine-growing region today, and towns like Avignon and Arles are built along its banks.

The river originates in the Swiss Alps and drains the Alpine region, connecting Swiss geography to France. The Rhône valley is central to southern French geography and culture. The river is the Alps' primary drainage to the Mediterranean, connecting alpine and Mediterranean worlds. Avignon, a major city on the Rhône, was the seat of the papacy in the fourteenth century. The Camargue, the river's wetland delta, is a unique European ecosystem that cannot be found elsewhere.
